1	# Cycle protocol
2	
3	This protocol uses [Prose form](prose.md#prose-form). It
4	contains instructions on how a commit cycle is accomplished.
5	
6	Universal file, shared with the template repository. A proposed
7	change is edited here and converges at the template
8	([Changing the agent-files](../AGENTS.md#changing-the-agent-files)).
9	Project-local content goes in [custom.md](../custom.md).
10	
11	The artifact a cycle produces is whatever the bot generates from
12	the conversation: code, prose, an image, a song, a screenplay.
13	The steps below use a Rust crate as the running example (the
14	cargo cycle, `Cargo.toml` versioning). Substitute your medium's
15	equivalents. This project's manifest is recorded in
16	[versioning.md](versioning.md).
17	
18	## Cycles
19	
20	A cycle has three phases:
21	
22	- **[Preparation](#preparation)**: the cycle's first commit,
23	  when it needs setup (a lightweight cycle omits it and
24	  starts at its first Work step). Sets up the cycle:
25	  - Bump the version-of-record (where it lives and the
26	    suffix scheme are project-specific, per
27	    [versioning.md](versioning.md)).
28	  - Pick up a `## Todo` item (typically the top-ranked, #1)
29	    into `## In Progress` as the cycle's
30	    [six provisional items](#preparation): title, problem
31	    statement, solution statement, acceptance check, ladder,
32	    deliberation.
33	  - Create the cycle's topic bookmark.
34	  - Nothing is opened in the chores file. The block is the
35	    cycle's only home until close-out moves it.
36	- **[Work-N](#work-n)**: the commits that implement the
37	  change. As many as the change needs. Each runs through the
38	  [per-commit flow](#per-commit-flow).
39	- **[Close-out](#close-out)**: the cycle's last commit.
40	  Bookkeeping only:
41	  - Run the acceptance check and record what it showed.
42	  - Finalize the six items, then move the block into
43	    `notes/chores/`, which creates the
44	    [chores section](#chores-sections).
45	  - Write the `## Done` entry and clear `## In Progress`.
46	  - Land the cycle's bookmark.
47	  - Optionally update `notes/README.md` if functionality
48	    changed.
49	
50	A cycle's commits are published to the project remote
51	either incrementally or as one batch at close-out. The
52	result must always be published at close-out. See
53	[Pushing](#pushing).
54	
55	**Sub-cycles.** When a Work commit's scope grows enough to
56	warrant its own ladder, it subdivides into its own
57	Preparation / Work / Close-out. The same three-phase shape
58	applies recursively at every depth, and a sub-ladder's rungs
59	are titles like any other. See
60	[Step naming](#step-naming) for how a step is identified and
61	[Sub-cycle ladders](#sub-cycle-ladders) for the local-ladder
62	mechanics.
63	
64	## Chores sections
65	
66	A **chores section** is a `##` section in `notes/chores/chores-NN.md` recording landed work.
67	In general, every commit that lands on the permanent branch should have a rung in some
68	section's as-built ladder in a chores file.
69	
70	**A cycle's record has one home at a time.** While the cycle runs it lives entirely in
71	`TODO.md > ## In Progress`, as the [six provisional items](#preparation) written at Preparation
72	and revised as steps land. At close-out the whole block **moves** into the chores file, becoming
73	that cycle's `##` section. It is never written in two places, so there is nothing to keep in
74	sync and nothing to write twice.
75	
76	The move is mechanical, four transforms and no rewriting:
77	
78	- **Heading levels shift so the title becomes the section's `##`** and the items shift with it,
79	  staying one level under the title. Anchors survive untouched, because GitHub slugs derive from
80	  the heading's *text*, not its level. The depth shift is one level for a plain cycle, and
81	  whatever the title's depth demands under a program heading.
82	- **Rung refs renumber** into the destination file's `[N]` namespace (see
83	  [Reference numbering](notes.md#reference-numbering)).
84	- **Repo-root-relative links gain `../`**, since the block moves from the root into
85	  `notes/chores/`.
86	- **The block's own forward-looking notes are rewritten**, since they described a future that
87	  has now happened.
88	
89	Two of those fail *silently*: a mis-renumbered ref and an un-rebased link render as plain text
90	or a 404 rather than erroring. Check both by hand until a `validate-repo` exists.
91	
92	A single-commit cycle's ladder is one rung, its close-out. Rung placeholders are backfilled once
93	the commit is permanent (see [Commits backfill](#commits-backfill) below).
94	
95	The move also appends the section's title-only `- [<title>](#<anchor>)` entry to the file's
96	`## Table of Contents`.
97	
98	Adopted after a full-cycle trial: the dual maintenance disappeared, and the narrative did not
99	thin out from being written in `TODO.md`, which was the watched-for risk.
100	
101	Fuller chores conventions (content rules, header sync, design subsection pattern, ladder and
102	reference formatting, the Table of Contents) live in
103	[Chores conventions](notes.md#chores-conventions).
104	
105	### Commits backfill
106	
107	An as-built ladder rung cites its commit by SHA and records the version that commit carried,
108	and neither is stable until the commit lands on a **permanent branch** (`main`, or a long-lived
109	release/patch branch that won't be rewritten). A rebase or squash rewrites the SHA and may
110	renumber the version on the way. So:
111	
112	- A rung is **written with the literal `[[N]]` placeholder and no version**.
113	- **Backfill once the commit is on a permanent branch**, where both are final. A commit
114	  can't record its own SHA (that would change the hash), so the fill always lands one push
115	  later: **each push backfills the rungs of the commits the previous push made permanent.** On
116	  a topic branch the sections instead wait until the branch lands, so nothing is ever written
117	  that a later rebase could invalidate.
118	- A deliberate rewrite of already-recorded commits (a coordinated re-describe, a retroactive
119	  reshape) invalidates their recorded SHAs. Re-record them once the rewrite is published, on
120	  the same one-push-later timing.
121	
122	Backfill replaces the placeholder with a real file-local `[N]` slot, defined as the commit URL +
123	40-hex SHA in the file's `# References` (format in
124	[Chores commit references](notes.md#chores-commit-references)), and writes the version ahead of
125	the title. A section's `##` title matches its close-out commit title, and each rung's text its
126	own commit title, so a rare deliberate rewrite of a permanent-branch commit re-syncs via
127	`git log --grep "<title>"`. Sections that predate the ladder form keep their grandfathered
128	`Commits:` lines. Backfill those where they exist.
129	
130	The per-push cadence is a project choice, not dogma. A **per-close-out** model (recording a
131	cycle's SHAs at its close-out) is equally valid. The one invariant: what a rung records must be
132	permanent.
133	
134	## Preparation
135	
136	The cycle's first commit, when the cycle needs setup (a
137	lightweight cycle omits it, per
138	[versioning.md](versioning.md#suffix-scheme)):
139	
140	- **Create the cycle's topic bookmark** (commands in
141	  [Cycle bookmarks](jj.md#cycle-bookmarks-create-and-land)).
142	- **Bump the version-of-record.** Where it lives, the suffix
143	  scheme, and any derived files (a lockfile, a sourced
144	  manifest version) are project-specific. See
145	  [versioning.md](versioning.md).
146	- **Move a `## Todo` item** (if the cycle has one) into
147	  `## In Progress`, and write the cycle's **six provisional
148	  items** there. All six are required, all six are revised
149	  as steps land, and all six move to chores at close-out.
150	  The title is a heading one level below `## In Progress`'s
151	  own, and the other five are headings one level below the
152	  title (a plain cycle: `###` title, `####` items; under a
153	  program heading, each one deeper):
154	  - the **title**, which becomes the chores section header.
155	  - the **problem statement**: what is wrong, in a sentence
156	    or two.
157	  - the **solution statement**: what will be done about it,
158	    broad. Provisional here, since it is written before the
159	    work. The close-out's commit body carries the final one.
160	  - the **acceptance check**: the measure of "are you
161	    finished?". Not the per-commit validation, which asks
162	    whether the artifact still works. This asks whether the
163	    thing the cycle promised actually happened, specifically
164	    enough that a reader can run it.
165	  - the **ladder**: one rung per step, a bare title plus a
166	    `(current)` / `(done)` marker.
167	  - the **deliberation**: how the five above were decided,
168	    alternatives weighed, costs accepted. `_None._` when
169	    there was nothing to deliberate, which is a real answer
170	    and different from having forgotten to write it.
171	
172	Nothing is opened in the chores file at Preparation. The
173	section is created at close-out by moving this block. See
174	[Chores sections](#chores-sections).
175	
176	**Why an acceptance check, and why it is provisional.** A
177	cycle's own per-commit checklists can all pass while its
178	banner claim is false: a seven-cycle program opened against
179	"end subprocess spawning" and its close-out claimed the goal
180	met, with about twenty spawn sites surviving, two inside the
181	facade the program built. Being provisional, the check can
182	also be revised *toward* what was achieved, which is the
183	same failure by a slower route. So a changed check is one of
184	the things the deliberation exists to justify.
185	
186	## Work-N
187	
188	The cycle's work commits (`X.Y.Z-1`, `X.Y.Z-2`, ...)
189	implement the change. As many as needed:
190	
191	- Each commit runs through the
192	  **[per-commit flow](#per-commit-flow)**.
193	- **Interim pushes** are optional (backup, progress
194	  visibility).
195	- Close-out is the only mandatory push (see
196	  [Pushing](#pushing)).
197	- **Subdivide into a sub-cycle** if a Work commit's
198	  scope grows enough (see
199	  [Sub-cycle ladders](#sub-cycle-ladders)).
200	
201	## Close-out
202	
203	The cycle's last commit does bookkeeping only, and the
204	commit body describes that bookkeeping, not what happens
205	post-squash:
206	
207	- **Run the acceptance check** the Preparation stated, and
208	  record what it showed in the block, whether or not it
209	  passed. A check that was never run is a failed close-out,
210	  and a check that failed is a finding, not a reason to
211	  quietly restate the banner.
212	- **Finalize the six items in place**, before the move: sync
213	  the title if the cycle's scope shifted (and every anchor
214	  back-reference), replace the provisional solution
215	  statement with what was actually done, drop the ladder's
216	  `(current)` / `(done)` markers since as-built implies
217	  done, and add any design subsections the deliberation
218	  grew.
219	- **Move the block** into `notes/chores/chores-NN.md`,
220	  applying the four transforms in
221	  [Chores sections](#chores-sections). This *creates* the
222	  section. Nothing was opened earlier.
223	- **Write the `## Done` entry**: the version, then a bold
224	  title line with its chores `[N]` ref and detail as
225	  sub-bullets (see
226	  [Done entry form](notes.md#done-entry-form)).
227	- **Replace the `## In Progress` cycle block** with
228	  `_No cycle currently in progress._`. Under a multi-cycle
229	  program (the program heading above the cycle title) this
230	  retires the cycle's block only. The program heading and
231	  its ladder stay, the shipped rung flipped `(done)`, so the
232	  marker sits inside the program block until the next stage
233	  is picked up.
234	- **Land the cycle's bookmark** on the user's go (commands
235	  in [Cycle bookmarks](jj.md#cycle-bookmarks-create-and-land)).
236	  Until this, nothing the cycle pushed is permanent. Landing
237	  triggers the backfill that waits on permanence.
238	- **Update `notes/README.md`** if functionality changed
239	  (new flags, new subcommands, changed behavior).
240	
241	Whether to **squash** the cycle into one commit before the
242	publishing push, or push as-is, is decided at push time. See
243	[Pushing](#pushing).
244	
245	## Step naming
246	
247	A step has a title and no number. The ladder lists its rungs
248	in order, so position is already recorded by the list, and a
249	step is referred to by its title, verbatim-identical in the
250	ladder rung, the chores `##` header and the commit (see
251	[Steps are named, not numbered](prose.md#steps-are-named-not-numbered)).
252	A title has to be unambiguous within its cycle and within
253	its chores file, where it is also an anchor. It may repeat
254	across the repo's history.
255	
256	The version-of-record still bumps for every step, and its
257	suffix still encodes the phase, but that encoding belongs to
258	the manifest and appears nowhere in prose. It is the one
259	number left in the system, it names nothing, and nothing
260	dereferences it. The full scheme (disambiguation, nesting,
261	optional Preparation, the project's version-of-record
262	format, and the per-step bump) lives in
263	[versioning.md](versioning.md#suffix-scheme), which is the
264	single source of truth for this repo's versioning.
265	
266	## Topic bookmarks are drafts
267	
268	A topic bookmark is a draft until it lands on a permanent
269	branch. Pushing to the bookmark makes the work durable and
270	visible; it does not publish it. Landing on the permanent
271	branch is publication, and that is the line the rules divide
272	at:
273	
274	- **Before landing**, the series should be self-consistent
275	  when practical. Inserting or reordering a step changes the
276	  ladder, and the rungs that already committed an older
277	  version of it are brought along, so the branch reads as
278	  one coherent ladder rather than a record of how it was
279	  assembled.
280	- **After landing**, the commits are history and are not
281	  touched. A recorded SHA is only ever written for a commit
282	  on a permanent branch (see
283	  [Commits backfill](#commits-backfill)), which is what
284	  makes rewriting a draft safe.
285	
286	Mechanics, and why they cost so little here:
287	
288	- **Amend content; never re-describe.** Editing `TODO.md`
289	  inside a rung and amending it is not a `jj describe`, so
290	  the never-re-describe rule stays intact. `ochid:` trailers
291	  survive, since they carry change ids rather than commit
292	  ids and a change id is stable across a rewrite.
293	- **Force-push the bookmark** afterwards, under the same
294	  approval any push needs.
295	- **Exceptions**, since "when practical" is not "always":
296	  the bookmark has already landed; another branch is stacked
297	  on it, so the rewrite becomes someone else's rebase; or
298	  the ladder is long and only a trailing snapshot disagrees.
299	  Name the reason and move on.
300	
301	A squash-form [sub-cycle ladder](#sub-cycle-ladders) never
302	meets this, because nothing on it is pushed and the
303	close-out squash collapses it. The rule is for the
304	multi-commit shape, whose rungs publish one at a time.
305	
306	## Per-commit flow
307	
308	Every commit (Preparation, each Work commit, Close-out) goes
309	through:
310	
311	1. **Mark this commit `(current)`** as the first edit in
312	   `TODO.md > ## In Progress` (`TODO.md` is at the repo
313	   root).
314	2. **Do the work** (see [Iterative work](#iterative-work)
315	   for the loop-and-squash technique).
316	3. **Flip this commit `(current)` -> `(done)`** in `## In
317	   Progress`, before the cargo cycle and the commit.
318	4. **Bump the version-of-record** to this commit's version
319	   (the suffix scheme is in
320	   [versioning.md](versioning.md#suffix-scheme)). The
321	   Preparation's own bump already covers a Preparation
322	   commit.
323	5. **Validate the artifact**, a medium-specific step, skip-able
324	   for notes-only commits, mandatory at close-out. For the Rust
325	   example the cargo cycle is:
326	   1. `cargo fmt`
327	   2. `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings`
328	   3. `cargo test`
329	   4. `cargo install --path . --locked`
330	   5. (re-test if anything substantive changed)
331	6. **Work review.** Stop *before* writing any description,
332	   and tell the user "ready to commit." The user reviews the
333	   changes and we iterate until complete.
334	7. **Write the commit description**. See
335	   [Commit description](#commit-description).
336	8. **Commit Description review.** Show the title + body
337	   and stop. The user reviews the description. Iterate.
338	9. **Commit + push.** Hand the approved title/body to
339	   `vc-x1 push <bookmark> --title "..." --body "..."`, whose
340	   commit stages commit both repos and stamp the `ochid:`
341	   trailers. Never pre-commit the rung with `jj commit`: an
342	   empty `@` at push mints a stamped empty duplicate.
343	   Push approval is per-push, so step 8's
344	   review covers it only when the user's go explicitly
345	   includes the push.
346	
347	**Two overrides apply:**
348	
349	- **Deviation or question.** Any time the work deviates
350	  from the agreed plan, or a question arises, stop and
351	  surface it. Don't push through.
352	- **ESC-ESC.** The user can interrupt at any point to pull
353	  a review or question forward.
354	
355	## Commit description
356	
357	[Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/):
358	
359	```
360	<type>: <short description>
361	<type>(scope): <short description>   # optional scope
362	```
363	
364	**A commit names no version**, in its title or its body. The
365	version-of-record (where it lives and its bump cadence, see
366	[versioning.md](versioning.md)) is useful for confirming you
367	are running the version you are testing. It is not an
368	identifier, and a commit already records it in the manifest.
369	Writing it into the description copies it into text that
370	cannot be edited: a version is only stable once it lands on
371	the permanent branch, and even then a history rewrite may
372	renumber it, at which point every description naming it is
373	wrong forever. See
374	[Versions live in the version-of-record only](prose.md#versions-live-in-the-version-of-record-only).
375	
376	### Title
377	
378	- <=50 chars total.
379	- Common types: `feat`, `fix`, `refactor`, `test`,
380	  `docs`, `chore`. Optional `(scope)` in parentheses after
381	  the type, per the spec.
382	- Favor terse phrasings.
383	- **Distinct per step.** Each of a cycle's commits gets its
384	  own descriptive title (no shared cycle title with a step
385	  marker). Share a greppable stem across the cycle's titles
386	  (e.g. `ring buffer`) so `git log --grep` collects them. The
387	  chores section header matches the close-out title. See
388	  [Conventional-commit shape](prose.md#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--chores--commit).
389	- **Unambiguous where it is resolved**: the title is the
390	  only identifier a record has, so it must be distinct
391	  within its cycle and within its chores file (a `##` header
392	  is also an anchor). It may repeat across the repo's
393	  history. See
394	  [Steps are named, not numbered](prose.md#steps-are-named-not-numbered).
395	
396	### Body
397	
398	A **problem statement** then a **solution statement**, in
399	[Prose form](prose.md#prose-form) (intro + bullets), wrapped
400	<=72. The problem statement says what was wrong and defines
401	any word the title assumes. The solution statement says what
402	was done about it. Content rules, including why the body
403	carries no file list, are in
404	[prose.md](prose.md#prose-form) and are not repeated here.
405	
406	Two repo-specific points:
407	
408	- **Work-repo body**: the problem is the artifact's or the
409	  records' problem.
410	- **Bot-repo (`.claude`) body**: the statements describe
411	  in-session activity rather than work-repo changes.
412	
413	### Trailer
414	
415	`ochid:` as the last line of the body. See
416	[Cross-repo linking (ochid trailers)](jj.md#cross-repo-linking-ochid-trailers)
417	in agent-data/jj.md for the convention.
418	
419	For breaking changes, use the hyphenated `BREAKING-CHANGE:`
420	trailer key. `BREAKING CHANGE:` (with a space) is the only
421	space-separated key the Conventional Commits spec allows. The
422	hyphenated form is also valid and avoids the space ambiguity.
423	
424	## Reviewing changes
425	
426	Work review looks at the **uncommitted working-copy diff**,
427	on the way to commit. The user opens diffs in their
428	editor (Zed, VSCode); jj commands are for terminal:
429	
430	- `jj diff`: working-copy diff (uncommitted)
431	- `jj diff -r @-`: diff of the previous commit
432	- `jj diff --from <X> --to <Y>`: any two revisions
433	- `jj show -r <X>`: description + diff for one rev
434	
435	Don't `jj edit -r @-` to view a past commit, because that marks
436	it mutable and shifts `@`. Use `jj diff -r @-` or
437	`jj show -r @-`.
438	
439	No preflight while a review iterates: `fmt` / `clippy` / `test`
440	wait until the review settles, since `fmt` mutates files in ways
441	that interact badly with the user's mid-review edits. Validation
442	runs once, on the settled state, per the per-commit checklist.
443	
444	See [Sub-cycle ladders](#sub-cycle-ladders) for the
445	close-out squash recipe and recovery. Revset primitives
446	are in [`jj.md > Revsets`](jj.md#revsets).
447	
448	## Pushing
449	
450	### Policy
451	
452	Push is **discretionary** during the cycle (backup,
453	progress visibility) and **mandatory at close-out**, since
454	the cycle's result must be published.
455	
456	**Approval is per-push.** Every push (any repo, any kind:
457	cycle push, interim backup, recovery/surgery force-push)
458	happens only after the user has reviewed the changes to be
459	published and explicitly approved that specific push.
460	Approval of a plan that *includes* a push does not authorize
461	the push itself. Stop and ask again at the moment of pushing.
462	
463	**Default is interactive; an explicit scoped delegation waives
464	the gates.** The gates above (per-push approval, the
465	commit-description review that shows title+body and stops, and
466	the hard stop after push/squash-push) are the *interactive
467	default*.
468	They yield when the user **explicitly** delegates a complete,
469	bounded task and authorizes carrying it through ("do all of X
470	and push each step, don't check in"). The bot then proceeds
471	through that task's commits and pushes without stopping, and
472	continues past each push to the next step. Conditions:
473	
474	- **Explicit grant.** Never inferred from a task merely being
475	  well-scoped. The user's words must authorize unattended
476	  completion. "Commit and push" (or "then push") names the
477	  destination, not a waiver: it authorizes the push *after*
478	  the normal work review and description review, not skipping
479	  them. Only wording that explicitly waives the stops ("don't
480	  check in", "no need to review", "carry it through
481	  unattended") waives them.
482	- **Bounded goal.** Covers the named task only. It does not
483	  carry to the next task or a vaguer follow-on.
484	- **Destructive ops still pause.** Delegation covers the task's
485	  ordinary commits and pushes. It does *not* pre-authorize a
486	  genuinely irreversible action (force-push over published
487	  history, history rewrite, deleting a remote branch). Those can
488	  permanently destroy work and aren't a normal cycle step, so the
489	  bot flags one before acting. An ordinary delegated cycle never
490	  reaches this.
491	- **Still transparent.** Report each commit/push as it lands
492	  (title + outcome) so the user can catch up.
493	- **When in doubt, ask.** Ambiguous authorization falls back to
494	  per-push approval.
495	
496	### Shape at close-out push
497	
498	At close-out the cycle's *work* is done; its *published
499	shape* is the remaining choice, made at push time. Surface
500	the options and get user approval before pushing. Once on
501	the target, changing shape is a remote rewrite (force-push,
502	needs approval), so choose deliberately.
503	
504	- **Squash to one commit**: single entry on the target.
505	  Right for straightforward changes where the Work-N is
506	  focused on one or two files.
507	- **Trapezoid** (a `git merge --no-ff` merge commit)
508	  *(current default)*: the target gains a merge commit
509	  (`X.Y.Z`) whose first parent is the trunk line and whose
510	  second parent is the cycle's ladder, so
511	  `git log --first-parent` reads one commit per cycle while
512	  every rung stays reachable. See
513	  [Trapezoid close-out recipe](#trapezoid-close-out-recipe)
514	  for the full sequence.
515	- **Keep separate**: one commit per cycle entry on
516	  `main`. Use when the decomposition itself is
517	  informative. Each chores section keeps its own header /
518	  ladder refs, no consolidation churn.
519	
520	A squash is set up before invoking `vc-x1 push`; a trapezoid
521	is reshaped between two pushes (the recipe below). For any
522	other shape, drive `jj git push` directly.
523	
524	### Trapezoid close-out recipe
525	
526	A [trapezoid](#shape-at-close-out-push) close-out is
527	published in four steps: an ordinary close-out push, a
528	two-command reshape, and a second push that re-points the
529	bookmark at the reshaped commit.
530	
531	```
532	  main line   ...──<base>──────────────────<closeout>──
533	                      \                    /
534	  ladder             <rung-1>──...──<tip>─┘
535	```
536	
537	- `<base>`: the **parent of the ladder's first rung**, which
538	  is the trunk position when the cycle opened. It becomes the
539	  first parent.
540	- `<tip>`: the cycle's last Work commit. It becomes the
541	  second parent.
542	- `<closeout>`: the close-out commit, created by step 1.
543	
544	The steps. Only step 1 is a `vc-x1 push`; the rest is jj,
545	because after step 1 the commits already exist and all that
546	remains is reshaping and publishing them:
547	
548	1. `vc-x1 push <bookmark> --title "..." --body "..."`
549	   - the ordinary close-out push. It commits both repos, stamps the
550	   `ochid:` trailers, and publishes `<closeout>` linearly.
551	2. `jj rebase -r <closeout> --onto <base> --onto <tip>`
552	   - `<closeout>` becomes the merge. Parent order is the
553	   argument order.
554	3. `jj new <closeout>`
555	   -  puts an empty `@` above the merge.
556	4. `jj git push --bookmark <bookmark> -R .`
557	   - publishes the reshaped commit. The bookmark needs no `jj bookmark set`:
558	   it follows the rewrite in step 2 automatically. The bot
559	   repo is untouched, and its session tail goes out with a
560	   separate `vc-x1 squash-push` afterwards.
561	
562	**Step 4 is not a `vc-x1 push`**, learned at a close-out
563	that tried it. Push runs its whole pipeline or
564	none of it, and the bot repo is never quiet for long: by the
565	time the reshape is done, `.claude` holds the session writes
566	from steps 1-3, so `commit-bot` wants to run and the message
567	stage demands a title for it. The result is a bot-side
568	requirement blocking a work-side publish that needs nothing
569	but a moved ref. Publishing an already-made commit is a
570	different operation from committing and publishing, and only
571	the latter is push's job.
572	
573	#### Details
574	
575	- **Verify two parents before step 4.** `jj log -r <closeout>
576	  -T 'parents.map(|p| p.change_id().short(8))'` must list
577	  both. jj preserves the second parent even though `<base>`
578	  is an ancestor of `<tip>` (observed at three consecutive
579	  close-outs), but a collapsed merge is indistinguishable from
580	  a correct one in `jj log --no-graph` and is only visible
581	  once published.
582	- **`<base>` is not always the previous close-out.** A docs
583	  or planning interlude between cycles sits on the trunk line
584	  and must stay there. Take the parent of the ladder's first
585	  rung, not the last close-out.
586	- **Step 3 is about `@`, not the bookmark.** The bookmark
587	  follows the rewrite in step 2 on its own. What step 2
588	  leaves misplaced is the working copy: `jj rebase -r`
589	  re-parents descendants onto the rebased commit's **old**
590	  parent, so the empty `@` from step 1 lands beside the merge
591	  on `<tip>`, and the working tree reverts to pre-close-out
592	  content, which looks alarming and isn't. `jj new` puts `@`
593	  back on top of the merge so the tree is right and the next
594	  commit continues from there. Skipping it doesn't break the
595	  publish; it leaves you working from the wrong parent.
596	- **Trailers survive.** The reshape changes `<closeout>`'s
597	  SHA but not its change ID, so the `ochid:` trailers stamped
598	  in step 1 stay valid in both directions. This is why the
599	  reshape is safe after the trailers are written.
600	- **Step 4 moves the bookmark sideways.** Step 1's SHA
601	  becomes unreachable, and anyone who fetched between the two
602	  pushes holds a dangling commit. Consequently a
603	  [Commits backfill](#commits-backfill) must never read a
604	  SHA from that window. Wait until step 4 lands.
605	- **Immutability.** No flag is needed on a long-lived topic
606	  bookmark. Only when `<closeout>` is already on `trunk()`
607	  does the rebase need `--ignore-immutable`, and then the
608	  push force-updates the target.
609	- **The bot repo is left for afterwards.** Step 4 touches only
610	  the work repo, so `.claude` still holds every session write
611	  from the whole procedure. `vc-x1 squash-push` folds that
612	  tail into the bot commit, and its change id survives the
613	  squash, so the work-side `ochid:` keeps resolving.
614	
615	#### Recovery
616	
617	- **Nothing is published between steps 2 and 3**, so the local
618	  reshape is undoable with `jj undo` / `jj op restore`.
619	- **A collapsed or mis-parented merge** (step 2 verification
620	  fails): undo and redo step 2 with the corrected revisions.
621	  Do not push a shape you did not intend. After step 4 the
622	  remote boundary is crossed and recovery is forward-only.
623	- **Working copy left beside the merge** (step 3 skipped):
624	  `jj new <closeout>` after the fact. Nothing published is
625	  affected (the bookmark was never wrong), but any commit
626	  made in the meantime branches off `<tip>` and needs a
627	  rebase onto the merge.
628	- **A wrong bookmark position**, however it arose:
629	  `jj bookmark set <bookmark> -r <closeout>` before pushing.
630	  If step 4 already published it, the fix is a second
631	  sideways move, not a rewrite.
632	
633	### vc-x1 push wrapper
634	
635	`vc-x1 push <bookmark>` wraps per-push mechanics. See
636	`vc-x1 push --help` for current flags. `<bookmark>` names a
637	work-repo bookmark only. The bot repo is always pinned to
638	`main` (see [.claude cadence](#claude-cadence)).
639	
640	**Current limitation**: only fully supports the
641	[Keep separate](#shape-at-close-out-push) shape. Other
642	shapes need manual jj steps. Planned improvements are
643	project state, tracked in the project's `TODO.md`.
644	This protocol describes only the stable mechanism.
645	
646	### .claude cadence
647	
648	**Cadence**: one push = one bot-repo commit, paired
649	with every work-repo commit in that push.
650	
651	The `.claude` working copy accumulates session data
652	across the cycle. Its change ID stays stable across
653	snapshots, `jj describe`, and the squash-push fold, so
654	work-repo `ochid:` trailers resolve.
655	
656	`.claude` is a linear journal: all session work lives
657	on `main`, regardless of the work-repo bookmark. **Do
658	not create or maintain bot-repo bookmarks that mirror
659	work-repo branches**, which risks the bot steering session
660	pushes to the wrong remote ref.
661	
662	Ending a session: if the user runs `/exit` there will be
663	session information created, which we don't worry about.
664	The user can close the terminal instead and `@` will
665	remain empty.
666	
667	### Bot communication at the reviews
668	
669	Use plain prose, no insider jargon ("Gate N signal",
670	"Checkpoint N", etc.):
671	
672	- **At Work review**, summarize what changed and stop.
673	  "Work complete. Please review."
674	- **At Commit Description review**, present `$TITLE`
675	  and `$BODY` explicitly, and ask permission to commit/push.
676	  Don't spell out the full `vc-x1 push ... --title ...
677	  --body ...` invocation by default.
678	- **At Post close-out review**, surface the shape
679	  options (squash / merge / keep) and the push target,
680	  then wait for the user's choice before any `jj squash` /
681	  `jj rebase` / `jj git push` invocation.
682	
683	### After push or squash-push: stop and wait
684	
685	After a **push** (crossing the remote boundary, by hand or
686	via the `vc-x1 push` wrapper, whose last stage publishes
687	the bot repo too) or a manual **squash-push** on the bot
688	repo, stop for the turn: no next step, edit, tool call, or
689	text output until the user directs otherwise. **Even when
690	the next step seems obvious, wait.**
691	
692	- **Scope**: the stop follows the user's directive, not the
693	  push. A standing directive covering more work ("finish
694	  the remaining ladder commits on your own") makes an
695	  intermediate push just a step; the hard stop lands on the
696	  turn's *final* push.
697	- **Why**: the bot repo is a live journal, so everything after
698	  the invocation (its own record, closing words) lands in
699	  `@` as a trailing tail. Between delegated pushes the tail
700	  rides into the next cycle's bot commit; the final push's
701	  tail has no next commit, and the bot's own squash-push is
702	  itself session data (`@` refills immediately), so only the
703	  user, after the turn, can capture it
704	  (`vc-x1 squash-push -R .claude`).
705	- **Silence**: put all closing words *before* the final
706	  push. The harness rejects an empty turn, so it may force a
707	  visible token after the tool returns. If so, emit a bare
708	  acknowledgment only (e.g. "landed"), never a summary,
709	  verification, or next-step offer. There is no "harmless"
710	  closing line after the push. That is a known slip.
711	- **Flush**: when the user wants `@` empty (no tail), they
712	  run `vc-x1 squash-push -R .claude` after the bot goes
713	  quiet, which flushes all bot session information into the
714	  published commit. Repeat if new writes land (see
715	  [Recovery](#recovery)).
716	
717	### Recovery
718	
719	- **If push exits before its last stage** (`push-work`
720	  succeeded but the bot-repo publish (`squash-push-bot`)
721	  didn't run), run the squash+push by hand:
722	
723	  ```
724	  vc-x1 squash-push -R .claude
725	  ```
726	
727	  It runs in-process, so a failure is a visible non-zero
728	  exit, with no log file to chase.
729	- **Run squash-push again if `@` is non-empty** after a
730	  pass (also desirable after extra activity by the bot's
731	  agents).
732	  - Why: the bot keeps writing session data while the
733	    command runs, so the invocation's own record plus any
734	    closing response land after the squash.
735	  - Safe to repeat: bot session data is append-only, so a
736	    re-run never conflicts or overwrites. (This could
737	    change. It is not under the user's control.)
738	  - No guarantees: events outside the bot's control can leave
739	    `@` non-empty. The bot's back end may decide to
740	    squash/consolidate session data, which can take minutes
741	    and land after the pass. The remedy is the same: just
742	    run squash-push again. This is why a single pass is never
743	    guaranteed to leave `@` empty.
744	- **Nothing to clear after an out-of-band recovery.** Push
745	  keeps no saved state, so whatever you do to the repos by
746	  hand is simply the state the next run sees.
747	- **Late work-repo tweak after the work-repo push succeeded**
748	  (e.g. updating AGENTS.md or memory) requires `jj
749	  squash --ignore-immutable` and a re-push. That is a
750	  remote rewrite and needs explicit approval like any
751	  push.
752	
753	## Iterative work
754	
755	When work for a single commit (the **target**) benefits
756	from incremental review, loop:
757	
758	1. `jj new -R .`: fresh empty `@` on top of the target.
759	2. Make the next round of changes.
760	3. User reviews the round (see
761	   [Reviewing changes](#reviewing-changes)).
762	4. `jj squash -R .` folds into the target and creates a
763	   new empty `@`.
764	5. If not done, go to step 2.
765	
766	Same jj mechanics as a
767	[sub-cycle ladder](#sub-cycle-ladders), but at
768	single-commit scope, so the version doesn't change.
769	
770	## Sub-cycle ladders
771	
772	When a Work commit subdivides into a sub-cycle (see
773	[Step naming](#step-naming), and
774	[versioning.md](versioning.md#suffix-scheme) for how the
775	manifest's suffix nests), its Work
776	commits will live as a local jj `@` chain and
777	**collapse into the sub-cycle's Close-out** before the
778	parent cycle continues. Ladder commits are scratch, for
779	review and bisection only.
780	
781	### Per-Work-commit contract within a ladder
782	
783	For each Work commit in the ladder:
784	
785	1. `jj new -R .`: create a fresh empty `@`.
786	2. Do the commit's work.
787	3. Run the fast validation (Rust example: `cargo test
788	   --bins`). **Non-negotiable**, because for code, build and
789	   clippy alone miss regressions until a later commit runs the
790	   full suite, raising bisection cost.
791	4. `jj describe -m "..." -m "..." -R .`: working title
792	   only. The sub-cycle Close-out collects everything
793	   into one final commit.
794	
795	**Nothing here is pushed.** The ladder is local until the
796	[Close-out squash](#close-out-squash-the-ladder), so no ladder
797	commit ever carries an `ochid:` trailer: the trailer is stamped
798	once, by `vc-x1 push`, on the squashed commit. Step 4 is
799	therefore first-time authoring of a scratch description, not a
800	rewrite of a published or stamped one, and is the named
801	exception to
802	[Re-describing](jj.md#re-describing-coordinate-first-and-keep-the-trailer).
803	
804	### Navigating the ladder
805	
806	Common moves:
807	
808	- `jj log -r '<base>::' -R .`: see the whole ladder
809	  from its base.
810	- `jj edit -r <prefix> -R .`: jump `@` to any ladder
811	  commit by chid prefix, useful for bisection.
812	- `jj edit @-- -R .`: quick-jump back two commits.
813	- `jj diff -r <chid> -R .`: review one commit in
814	  isolation.
815	
816	Modifications to any ladder commit rewrite it in place, and
817	descendants auto-rebase.
818	
819	### Close-out: squash the ladder
820	
821	When all ladder Work commits are done and tests pass:
822	
823	```
824	jj squash --from "<base>..@-" --into @ -u -R .
825	```
826	
827	`<base>` is the parent of the first ladder commit, and `-u`
828	keeps `@`'s description and discards the sources'.
829	After squash, history is linear (`<base> -> @`), and
830	intermediate commits are auto-abandoned.
831	
832	Then `vc-x1 push <bookmark>` as for any other commit. This is
833	the ladder's first and only publish, and where its `ochid:`
834	trailer is stamped. The scratch descriptions written at step 4
835	of the
836	[per-Work-commit contract](#per-work-commit-contract-within-a-ladder)
837	never left the machine and never carried one, which is why
838	describing them freely is safe.
839	
840	For N = 1 the squash is a no-op (`<base>..@-` is empty
841	when `@-` is `<base>`). Push the single commit directly.
842	
843	### Recovery
844	
845	If a ladder commit goes wrong, back out without losing
846	prior commits:
847	
848	- **Discard the current commit.** `jj abandon @ -R .`
849	  drops it, and you get a fresh empty `@` on the same
850	  parent.
851	- **Edit an earlier commit.** `jj edit -r <chid> -R .`,
852	  make corrections, then `jj edit -r <last-ladder-chid>`
853	  to return. Descendants auto-rebase.
854	- **Discard the entire ladder.** `jj op log -R .` shows
855	  the op history, and `jj op restore <op-id> -R .` reverts
856	  to that point. Full undo: removes *all* ladder work
857	  after the chosen op. Use only to start over.
858	
859	# References
860	
861	- [`jj.md > Revsets`](jj.md#revsets): revset primitives
862	  (chid/cid, `@`/`@-`/`@+`, `..`/`::` ranges, prefix matching).
863	- The per-commit `cargo test --bins` gate exists because a
864	  regression introduced in an early ladder commit can go
865	  uncaught until a later commit runs the full suite, raising
866	  bisection cost.
867

file.content:
# Cycle protocol

This protocol uses [Prose form](prose.md#prose-form). It
contains instructions on how a commit cycle is accomplished.

Universal file, shared with the template repository. A proposed
change is edited here and converges at the template
([Changing the agent-files](../AGENTS.md#changing-the-agent-files)).
Project-local content goes in [custom.md](../custom.md).

The artifact a cycle produces is whatever the bot generates from
the conversation: code, prose, an image, a song, a screenplay.
The steps below use a Rust crate as the running example (the
cargo cycle, `Cargo.toml` versioning). Substitute your medium's
equivalents. This project's manifest is recorded in
[versioning.md](versioning.md).

## Cycles

A cycle has three phases:

- **[Preparation](#preparation)**: the cycle's first commit,
  when it needs setup (a lightweight cycle omits it and
  starts at its first Work step). Sets up the cycle:
  - Bump the version-of-record (where it lives and the
    suffix scheme are project-specific, per
    [versioning.md](versioning.md)).
  - Pick up a `## Todo` item (typically the top-ranked, #1)
    into `## In Progress` as the cycle's
    [six provisional items](#preparation): title, problem
    statement, solution statement, acceptance check, ladder,
    deliberation.
  - Create the cycle's topic bookmark.
  - Nothing is opened in the chores file. The block is the
    cycle's only home until close-out moves it.
- **[Work-N](#work-n)**: the commits that implement the
  change. As many as the change needs. Each runs through the
  [per-commit flow](#per-commit-flow).
- **[Close-out](#close-out)**: the cycle's last commit.
  Bookkeeping only:
  - Run the acceptance check and record what it showed.
  - Finalize the six items, then move the block into
    `notes/chores/`, which creates the
    [chores section](#chores-sections).
  - Write the `## Done` entry and clear `## In Progress`.
  - Land the cycle's bookmark.
  - Optionally update `notes/README.md` if functionality
    changed.

A cycle's commits are published to the project remote
either incrementally or as one batch at close-out. The
result must always be published at close-out. See
[Pushing](#pushing).

**Sub-cycles.** When a Work commit's scope grows enough to
warrant its own ladder, it subdivides into its own
Preparation / Work / Close-out. The same three-phase shape
applies recursively at every depth, and a sub-ladder's rungs
are titles like any other. See
[Step naming](#step-naming) for how a step is identified and
[Sub-cycle ladders](#sub-cycle-ladders) for the local-ladder
mechanics.

## Chores sections

A **chores section** is a `##` section in `notes/chores/chores-NN.md` recording landed work.
In general, every commit that lands on the permanent branch should have a rung in some
section's as-built ladder in a chores file.

**A cycle's record has one home at a time.** While the cycle runs it lives entirely in
`TODO.md > ## In Progress`, as the [six provisional items](#preparation) written at Preparation
and revised as steps land. At close-out the whole block **moves** into the chores file, becoming
that cycle's `##` section. It is never written in two places, so there is nothing to keep in
sync and nothing to write twice.

The move is mechanical, four transforms and no rewriting:

- **Heading levels shift so the title becomes the section's `##`** and the items shift with it,
  staying one level under the title. Anchors survive untouched, because GitHub slugs derive from
  the heading's *text*, not its level. The depth shift is one level for a plain cycle, and
  whatever the title's depth demands under a program heading.
- **Rung refs renumber** into the destination file's `[N]` namespace (see
  [Reference numbering](notes.md#reference-numbering)).
- **Repo-root-relative links gain `../`**, since the block moves from the root into
  `notes/chores/`.
- **The block's own forward-looking notes are rewritten**, since they described a future that
  has now happened.

Two of those fail *silently*: a mis-renumbered ref and an un-rebased link render as plain text
or a 404 rather than erroring. Check both by hand until a `validate-repo` exists.

A single-commit cycle's ladder is one rung, its close-out. Rung placeholders are backfilled once
the commit is permanent (see [Commits backfill](#commits-backfill) below).

The move also appends the section's title-only `- [<title>](#<anchor>)` entry to the file's
`## Table of Contents`.

Adopted after a full-cycle trial: the dual maintenance disappeared, and the narrative did not
thin out from being written in `TODO.md`, which was the watched-for risk.

Fuller chores conventions (content rules, header sync, design subsection pattern, ladder and
reference formatting, the Table of Contents) live in
[Chores conventions](notes.md#chores-conventions).

### Commits backfill

An as-built ladder rung cites its commit by SHA and records the version that commit carried,
and neither is stable until the commit lands on a **permanent branch** (`main`, or a long-lived
release/patch branch that won't be rewritten). A rebase or squash rewrites the SHA and may
renumber the version on the way. So:

- A rung is **written with the literal `[[N]]` placeholder and no version**.
- **Backfill once the commit is on a permanent branch**, where both are final. A commit
  can't record its own SHA (that would change the hash), so the fill always lands one push
  later: **each push backfills the rungs of the commits the previous push made permanent.** On
  a topic branch the sections instead wait until the branch lands, so nothing is ever written
  that a later rebase could invalidate.
- A deliberate rewrite of already-recorded commits (a coordinated re-describe, a retroactive
  reshape) invalidates their recorded SHAs. Re-record them once the rewrite is published, on
  the same one-push-later timing.

Backfill replaces the placeholder with a real file-local `[N]` slot, defined as the commit URL +
40-hex SHA in the file's `# References` (format in
[Chores commit references](notes.md#chores-commit-references)), and writes the version ahead of
the title. A section's `##` title matches its close-out commit title, and each rung's text its
own commit title, so a rare deliberate rewrite of a permanent-branch commit re-syncs via
`git log --grep "<title>"`. Sections that predate the ladder form keep their grandfathered
`Commits:` lines. Backfill those where they exist.

The per-push cadence is a project choice, not dogma. A **per-close-out** model (recording a
cycle's SHAs at its close-out) is equally valid. The one invariant: what a rung records must be
permanent.

## Preparation

The cycle's first commit, when the cycle needs setup (a
lightweight cycle omits it, per
[versioning.md](versioning.md#suffix-scheme)):

- **Create the cycle's topic bookmark** (commands in
  [Cycle bookmarks](jj.md#cycle-bookmarks-create-and-land)).
- **Bump the version-of-record.** Where it lives, the suffix
  scheme, and any derived files (a lockfile, a sourced
  manifest version) are project-specific. See
  [versioning.md](versioning.md).
- **Move a `## Todo` item** (if the cycle has one) into
  `## In Progress`, and write the cycle's **six provisional
  items** there. All six are required, all six are revised
  as steps land, and all six move to chores at close-out.
  The title is a heading one level below `## In Progress`'s
  own, and the other five are headings one level below the
  title (a plain cycle: `###` title, `####` items; under a
  program heading, each one deeper):
  - the **title**, which becomes the chores section header.
  - the **problem statement**: what is wrong, in a sentence
    or two.
  - the **solution statement**: what will be done about it,
    broad. Provisional here, since it is written before the
    work. The close-out's commit body carries the final one.
  - the **acceptance check**: the measure of "are you
    finished?". Not the per-commit validation, which asks
    whether the artifact still works. This asks whether the
    thing the cycle promised actually happened, specifically
    enough that a reader can run it.
  - the **ladder**: one rung per step, a bare title plus a
    `(current)` / `(done)` marker.
  - the **deliberation**: how the five above were decided,
    alternatives weighed, costs accepted. `_None._` when
    there was nothing to deliberate, which is a real answer
    and different from having forgotten to write it.

Nothing is opened in the chores file at Preparation. The
section is created at close-out by moving this block. See
[Chores sections](#chores-sections).

**Why an acceptance check, and why it is provisional.** A
cycle's own per-commit checklists can all pass while its
banner claim is false: a seven-cycle program opened against
"end subprocess spawning" and its close-out claimed the goal
met, with about twenty spawn sites surviving, two inside the
facade the program built. Being provisional, the check can
also be revised *toward* what was achieved, which is the
same failure by a slower route. So a changed check is one of
the things the deliberation exists to justify.

## Work-N

The cycle's work commits (`X.Y.Z-1`, `X.Y.Z-2`, ...)
implement the change. As many as needed:

- Each commit runs through the
  **[per-commit flow](#per-commit-flow)**.
- **Interim pushes** are optional (backup, progress
  visibility).
- Close-out is the only mandatory push (see
  [Pushing](#pushing)).
- **Subdivide into a sub-cycle** if a Work commit's
  scope grows enough (see
  [Sub-cycle ladders](#sub-cycle-ladders)).

## Close-out

The cycle's last commit does bookkeeping only, and the
commit body describes that bookkeeping, not what happens
post-squash:

- **Run the acceptance check** the Preparation stated, and
  record what it showed in the block, whether or not it
  passed. A check that was never run is a failed close-out,
  and a check that failed is a finding, not a reason to
  quietly restate the banner.
- **Finalize the six items in place**, before the move: sync
  the title if the cycle's scope shifted (and every anchor
  back-reference), replace the provisional solution
  statement with what was actually done, drop the ladder's
  `(current)` / `(done)` markers since as-built implies
  done, and add any design subsections the deliberation
  grew.
- **Move the block** into `notes/chores/chores-NN.md`,
  applying the four transforms in
  [Chores sections](#chores-sections). This *creates* the
  section. Nothing was opened earlier.
- **Write the `## Done` entry**: the version, then a bold
  title line with its chores `[N]` ref and detail as
  sub-bullets (see
  [Done entry form](notes.md#done-entry-form)).
- **Replace the `## In Progress` cycle block** with
  `_No cycle currently in progress._`. Under a multi-cycle
  program (the program heading above the cycle title) this
  retires the cycle's block only. The program heading and
  its ladder stay, the shipped rung flipped `(done)`, so the
  marker sits inside the program block until the next stage
  is picked up.
- **Land the cycle's bookmark** on the user's go (commands
  in [Cycle bookmarks](jj.md#cycle-bookmarks-create-and-land)).
  Until this, nothing the cycle pushed is permanent. Landing
  triggers the backfill that waits on permanence.
- **Update `notes/README.md`** if functionality changed
  (new flags, new subcommands, changed behavior).

Whether to **squash** the cycle into one commit before the
publishing push, or push as-is, is decided at push time. See
[Pushing](#pushing).

## Step naming

A step has a title and no number. The ladder lists its rungs
in order, so position is already recorded by the list, and a
step is referred to by its title, verbatim-identical in the
ladder rung, the chores `##` header and the commit (see
[Steps are named, not numbered](prose.md#steps-are-named-not-numbered)).
A title has to be unambiguous within its cycle and within
its chores file, where it is also an anchor. It may repeat
across the repo's history.

The version-of-record still bumps for every step, and its
suffix still encodes the phase, but that encoding belongs to
the manifest and appears nowhere in prose. It is the one
number left in the system, it names nothing, and nothing
dereferences it. The full scheme (disambiguation, nesting,
optional Preparation, the project's version-of-record
format, and the per-step bump) lives in
[versioning.md](versioning.md#suffix-scheme), which is the
single source of truth for this repo's versioning.

## Topic bookmarks are drafts

A topic bookmark is a draft until it lands on a permanent
branch. Pushing to the bookmark makes the work durable and
visible; it does not publish it. Landing on the permanent
branch is publication, and that is the line the rules divide
at:

- **Before landing**, the series should be self-consistent
  when practical. Inserting or reordering a step changes the
  ladder, and the rungs that already committed an older
  version of it are brought along, so the branch reads as
  one coherent ladder rather than a record of how it was
  assembled.
- **After landing**, the commits are history and are not
  touched. A recorded SHA is only ever written for a commit
  on a permanent branch (see
  [Commits backfill](#commits-backfill)), which is what
  makes rewriting a draft safe.

Mechanics, and why they cost so little here:

- **Amend content; never re-describe.** Editing `TODO.md`
  inside a rung and amending it is not a `jj describe`, so
  the never-re-describe rule stays intact. `ochid:` trailers
  survive, since they carry change ids rather than commit
  ids and a change id is stable across a rewrite.
- **Force-push the bookmark** afterwards, under the same
  approval any push needs.
- **Exceptions**, since "when practical" is not "always":
  the bookmark has already landed; another branch is stacked
  on it, so the rewrite becomes someone else's rebase; or
  the ladder is long and only a trailing snapshot disagrees.
  Name the reason and move on.

A squash-form [sub-cycle ladder](#sub-cycle-ladders) never
meets this, because nothing on it is pushed and the
close-out squash collapses it. The rule is for the
multi-commit shape, whose rungs publish one at a time.

## Per-commit flow

Every commit (Preparation, each Work commit, Close-out) goes
through:

1. **Mark this commit `(current)`** as the first edit in
   `TODO.md > ## In Progress` (`TODO.md` is at the repo
   root).
2. **Do the work** (see [Iterative work](#iterative-work)
   for the loop-and-squash technique).
3. **Flip this commit `(current)` -> `(done)`** in `## In
   Progress`, before the cargo cycle and the commit.
4. **Bump the version-of-record** to this commit's version
   (the suffix scheme is in
   [versioning.md](versioning.md#suffix-scheme)). The
   Preparation's own bump already covers a Preparation
   commit.
5. **Validate the artifact**, a medium-specific step, skip-able
   for notes-only commits, mandatory at close-out. For the Rust
   example the cargo cycle is:
   1. `cargo fmt`
   2. `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings`
   3. `cargo test`
   4. `cargo install --path . --locked`
   5. (re-test if anything substantive changed)
6. **Work review.** Stop *before* writing any description,
   and tell the user "ready to commit." The user reviews the
   changes and we iterate until complete.
7. **Write the commit description**. See
   [Commit description](#commit-description).
8. **Commit Description review.** Show the title + body
   and stop. The user reviews the description. Iterate.
9. **Commit + push.** Hand the approved title/body to
   `vc-x1 push <bookmark> --title "..." --body "..."`, whose
   commit stages commit both repos and stamp the `ochid:`
   trailers. Never pre-commit the rung with `jj commit`: an
   empty `@` at push mints a stamped empty duplicate.
   Push approval is per-push, so step 8's
   review covers it only when the user's go explicitly
   includes the push.

**Two overrides apply:**

- **Deviation or question.** Any time the work deviates
  from the agreed plan, or a question arises, stop and
  surface it. Don't push through.
- **ESC-ESC.** The user can interrupt at any point to pull
  a review or question forward.

## Commit description

[Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/):

```
<type>: <short description>
<type>(scope): <short description>   # optional scope
```

**A commit names no version**, in its title or its body. The
version-of-record (where it lives and its bump cadence, see
[versioning.md](versioning.md)) is useful for confirming you
are running the version you are testing. It is not an
identifier, and a commit already records it in the manifest.
Writing it into the description copies it into text that
cannot be edited: a version is only stable once it lands on
the permanent branch, and even then a history rewrite may
renumber it, at which point every description naming it is
wrong forever. See
[Versions live in the version-of-record only](prose.md#versions-live-in-the-version-of-record-only).

### Title

- <=50 chars total.
- Common types: `feat`, `fix`, `refactor`, `test`,
  `docs`, `chore`. Optional `(scope)` in parentheses after
  the type, per the spec.
- Favor terse phrasings.
- **Distinct per step.** Each of a cycle's commits gets its
  own descriptive title (no shared cycle title with a step
  marker). Share a greppable stem across the cycle's titles
  (e.g. `ring buffer`) so `git log --grep` collects them. The
  chores section header matches the close-out title. See
  [Conventional-commit shape](prose.md#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--chores--commit).
- **Unambiguous where it is resolved**: the title is the
  only identifier a record has, so it must be distinct
  within its cycle and within its chores file (a `##` header
  is also an anchor). It may repeat across the repo's
  history. See
  [Steps are named, not numbered](prose.md#steps-are-named-not-numbered).

### Body

A **problem statement** then a **solution statement**, in
[Prose form](prose.md#prose-form) (intro + bullets), wrapped
<=72. The problem statement says what was wrong and defines
any word the title assumes. The solution statement says what
was done about it. Content rules, including why the body
carries no file list, are in
[prose.md](prose.md#prose-form) and are not repeated here.

Two repo-specific points:

- **Work-repo body**: the problem is the artifact's or the
  records' problem.
- **Bot-repo (`.claude`) body**: the statements describe
  in-session activity rather than work-repo changes.

### Trailer

`ochid:` as the last line of the body. See
[Cross-repo linking (ochid trailers)](jj.md#cross-repo-linking-ochid-trailers)
in agent-data/jj.md for the convention.

For breaking changes, use the hyphenated `BREAKING-CHANGE:`
trailer key. `BREAKING CHANGE:` (with a space) is the only
space-separated key the Conventional Commits spec allows. The
hyphenated form is also valid and avoids the space ambiguity.

## Reviewing changes

Work review looks at the **uncommitted working-copy diff**,
on the way to commit. The user opens diffs in their
editor (Zed, VSCode); jj commands are for terminal:

- `jj diff`: working-copy diff (uncommitted)
- `jj diff -r @-`: diff of the previous commit
- `jj diff --from <X> --to <Y>`: any two revisions
- `jj show -r <X>`: description + diff for one rev

Don't `jj edit -r @-` to view a past commit, because that marks
it mutable and shifts `@`. Use `jj diff -r @-` or
`jj show -r @-`.

No preflight while a review iterates: `fmt` / `clippy` / `test`
wait until the review settles, since `fmt` mutates files in ways
that interact badly with the user's mid-review edits. Validation
runs once, on the settled state, per the per-commit checklist.

See [Sub-cycle ladders](#sub-cycle-ladders) for the
close-out squash recipe and recovery. Revset primitives
are in [`jj.md > Revsets`](jj.md#revsets).

## Pushing

### Policy

Push is **discretionary** during the cycle (backup,
progress visibility) and **mandatory at close-out**, since
the cycle's result must be published.

**Approval is per-push.** Every push (any repo, any kind:
cycle push, interim backup, recovery/surgery force-push)
happens only after the user has reviewed the changes to be
published and explicitly approved that specific push.
Approval of a plan that *includes* a push does not authorize
the push itself. Stop and ask again at the moment of pushing.

**Default is interactive; an explicit scoped delegation waives
the gates.** The gates above (per-push approval, the
commit-description review that shows title+body and stops, and
the hard stop after push/squash-push) are the *interactive
default*.
They yield when the user **explicitly** delegates a complete,
bounded task and authorizes carrying it through ("do all of X
and push each step, don't check in"). The bot then proceeds
through that task's commits and pushes without stopping, and
continues past each push to the next step. Conditions:

- **Explicit grant.** Never inferred from a task merely being
  well-scoped. The user's words must authorize unattended
  completion. "Commit and push" (or "then push") names the
  destination, not a waiver: it authorizes the push *after*
  the normal work review and description review, not skipping
  them. Only wording that explicitly waives the stops ("don't
  check in", "no need to review", "carry it through
  unattended") waives them.
- **Bounded goal.** Covers the named task only. It does not
  carry to the next task or a vaguer follow-on.
- **Destructive ops still pause.** Delegation covers the task's
  ordinary commits and pushes. It does *not* pre-authorize a
  genuinely irreversible action (force-push over published
  history, history rewrite, deleting a remote branch). Those can
  permanently destroy work and aren't a normal cycle step, so the
  bot flags one before acting. An ordinary delegated cycle never
  reaches this.
- **Still transparent.** Report each commit/push as it lands
  (title + outcome) so the user can catch up.
- **When in doubt, ask.** Ambiguous authorization falls back to
  per-push approval.

### Shape at close-out push

At close-out the cycle's *work* is done; its *published
shape* is the remaining choice, made at push time. Surface
the options and get user approval before pushing. Once on
the target, changing shape is a remote rewrite (force-push,
needs approval), so choose deliberately.

- **Squash to one commit**: single entry on the target.
  Right for straightforward changes where the Work-N is
  focused on one or two files.
- **Trapezoid** (a `git merge --no-ff` merge commit)
  *(current default)*: the target gains a merge commit
  (`X.Y.Z`) whose first parent is the trunk line and whose
  second parent is the cycle's ladder, so
  `git log --first-parent` reads one commit per cycle while
  every rung stays reachable. See
  [Trapezoid close-out recipe](#trapezoid-close-out-recipe)
  for the full sequence.
- **Keep separate**: one commit per cycle entry on
  `main`. Use when the decomposition itself is
  informative. Each chores section keeps its own header /
  ladder refs, no consolidation churn.

A squash is set up before invoking `vc-x1 push`; a trapezoid
is reshaped between two pushes (the recipe below). For any
other shape, drive `jj git push` directly.

### Trapezoid close-out recipe

A [trapezoid](#shape-at-close-out-push) close-out is
published in four steps: an ordinary close-out push, a
two-command reshape, and a second push that re-points the
bookmark at the reshaped commit.

```
  main line   ...──<base>──────────────────<closeout>──
                      \                    /
  ladder             <rung-1>──...──<tip>─┘
```

- `<base>`: the **parent of the ladder's first rung**, which
  is the trunk position when the cycle opened. It becomes the
  first parent.
- `<tip>`: the cycle's last Work commit. It becomes the
  second parent.
- `<closeout>`: the close-out commit, created by step 1.

The steps. Only step 1 is a `vc-x1 push`; the rest is jj,
because after step 1 the commits already exist and all that
remains is reshaping and publishing them:

1. `vc-x1 push <bookmark> --title "..." --body "..."`
   - the ordinary close-out push. It commits both repos, stamps the
   `ochid:` trailers, and publishes `<closeout>` linearly.
2. `jj rebase -r <closeout> --onto <base> --onto <tip>`
   - `<closeout>` becomes the merge. Parent order is the
   argument order.
3. `jj new <closeout>`
   -  puts an empty `@` above the merge.
4. `jj git push --bookmark <bookmark> -R .`
   - publishes the reshaped commit. The bookmark needs no `jj bookmark set`:
   it follows the rewrite in step 2 automatically. The bot
   repo is untouched, and its session tail goes out with a
   separate `vc-x1 squash-push` afterwards.

**Step 4 is not a `vc-x1 push`**, learned at a close-out
that tried it. Push runs its whole pipeline or
none of it, and the bot repo is never quiet for long: by the
time the reshape is done, `.claude` holds the session writes
from steps 1-3, so `commit-bot` wants to run and the message
stage demands a title for it. The result is a bot-side
requirement blocking a work-side publish that needs nothing
but a moved ref. Publishing an already-made commit is a
different operation from committing and publishing, and only
the latter is push's job.

#### Details

- **Verify two parents before step 4.** `jj log -r <closeout>
  -T 'parents.map(|p| p.change_id().short(8))'` must list
  both. jj preserves the second parent even though `<base>`
  is an ancestor of `<tip>` (observed at three consecutive
  close-outs), but a collapsed merge is indistinguishable from
  a correct one in `jj log --no-graph` and is only visible
  once published.
- **`<base>` is not always the previous close-out.** A docs
  or planning interlude between cycles sits on the trunk line
  and must stay there. Take the parent of the ladder's first
  rung, not the last close-out.
- **Step 3 is about `@`, not the bookmark.** The bookmark
  follows the rewrite in step 2 on its own. What step 2
  leaves misplaced is the working copy: `jj rebase -r`
  re-parents descendants onto the rebased commit's **old**
  parent, so the empty `@` from step 1 lands beside the merge
  on `<tip>`, and the working tree reverts to pre-close-out
  content, which looks alarming and isn't. `jj new` puts `@`
  back on top of the merge so the tree is right and the next
  commit continues from there. Skipping it doesn't break the
  publish; it leaves you working from the wrong parent.
- **Trailers survive.** The reshape changes `<closeout>`'s
  SHA but not its change ID, so the `ochid:` trailers stamped
  in step 1 stay valid in both directions. This is why the
  reshape is safe after the trailers are written.
- **Step 4 moves the bookmark sideways.** Step 1's SHA
  becomes unreachable, and anyone who fetched between the two
  pushes holds a dangling commit. Consequently a
  [Commits backfill](#commits-backfill) must never read a
  SHA from that window. Wait until step 4 lands.
- **Immutability.** No flag is needed on a long-lived topic
  bookmark. Only when `<closeout>` is already on `trunk()`
  does the rebase need `--ignore-immutable`, and then the
  push force-updates the target.
- **The bot repo is left for afterwards.** Step 4 touches only
  the work repo, so `.claude` still holds every session write
  from the whole procedure. `vc-x1 squash-push` folds that
  tail into the bot commit, and its change id survives the
  squash, so the work-side `ochid:` keeps resolving.

#### Recovery

- **Nothing is published between steps 2 and 3**, so the local
  reshape is undoable with `jj undo` / `jj op restore`.
- **A collapsed or mis-parented merge** (step 2 verification
  fails): undo and redo step 2 with the corrected revisions.
  Do not push a shape you did not intend. After step 4 the
  remote boundary is crossed and recovery is forward-only.
- **Working copy left beside the merge** (step 3 skipped):
  `jj new <closeout>` after the fact. Nothing published is
  affected (the bookmark was never wrong), but any commit
  made in the meantime branches off `<tip>` and needs a
  rebase onto the merge.
- **A wrong bookmark position**, however it arose:
  `jj bookmark set <bookmark> -r <closeout>` before pushing.
  If step 4 already published it, the fix is a second
  sideways move, not a rewrite.

### vc-x1 push wrapper

`vc-x1 push <bookmark>` wraps per-push mechanics. See
`vc-x1 push --help` for current flags. `<bookmark>` names a
work-repo bookmark only. The bot repo is always pinned to
`main` (see [.claude cadence](#claude-cadence)).

**Current limitation**: only fully supports the
[Keep separate](#shape-at-close-out-push) shape. Other
shapes need manual jj steps. Planned improvements are
project state, tracked in the project's `TODO.md`.
This protocol describes only the stable mechanism.

### .claude cadence

**Cadence**: one push = one bot-repo commit, paired
with every work-repo commit in that push.

The `.claude` working copy accumulates session data
across the cycle. Its change ID stays stable across
snapshots, `jj describe`, and the squash-push fold, so
work-repo `ochid:` trailers resolve.

`.claude` is a linear journal: all session work lives
on `main`, regardless of the work-repo bookmark. **Do
not create or maintain bot-repo bookmarks that mirror
work-repo branches**, which risks the bot steering session
pushes to the wrong remote ref.

Ending a session: if the user runs `/exit` there will be
session information created, which we don't worry about.
The user can close the terminal instead and `@` will
remain empty.

### Bot communication at the reviews

Use plain prose, no insider jargon ("Gate N signal",
"Checkpoint N", etc.):

- **At Work review**, summarize what changed and stop.
  "Work complete. Please review."
- **At Commit Description review**, present `$TITLE`
  and `$BODY` explicitly, and ask permission to commit/push.
  Don't spell out the full `vc-x1 push ... --title ...
  --body ...` invocation by default.
- **At Post close-out review**, surface the shape
  options (squash / merge / keep) and the push target,
  then wait for the user's choice before any `jj squash` /
  `jj rebase` / `jj git push` invocation.

### After push or squash-push: stop and wait

After a **push** (crossing the remote boundary, by hand or
via the `vc-x1 push` wrapper, whose last stage publishes
the bot repo too) or a manual **squash-push** on the bot
repo, stop for the turn: no next step, edit, tool call, or
text output until the user directs otherwise. **Even when
the next step seems obvious, wait.**

- **Scope**: the stop follows the user's directive, not the
  push. A standing directive covering more work ("finish
  the remaining ladder commits on your own") makes an
  intermediate push just a step; the hard stop lands on the
  turn's *final* push.
- **Why**: the bot repo is a live journal, so everything after
  the invocation (its own record, closing words) lands in
  `@` as a trailing tail. Between delegated pushes the tail
  rides into the next cycle's bot commit; the final push's
  tail has no next commit, and the bot's own squash-push is
  itself session data (`@` refills immediately), so only the
  user, after the turn, can capture it
  (`vc-x1 squash-push -R .claude`).
- **Silence**: put all closing words *before* the final
  push. The harness rejects an empty turn, so it may force a
  visible token after the tool returns. If so, emit a bare
  acknowledgment only (e.g. "landed"), never a summary,
  verification, or next-step offer. There is no "harmless"
  closing line after the push. That is a known slip.
- **Flush**: when the user wants `@` empty (no tail), they
  run `vc-x1 squash-push -R .claude` after the bot goes
  quiet, which flushes all bot session information into the
  published commit. Repeat if new writes land (see
  [Recovery](#recovery)).

### Recovery

- **If push exits before its last stage** (`push-work`
  succeeded but the bot-repo publish (`squash-push-bot`)
  didn't run), run the squash+push by hand:

  ```
  vc-x1 squash-push -R .claude
  ```

  It runs in-process, so a failure is a visible non-zero
  exit, with no log file to chase.
- **Run squash-push again if `@` is non-empty** after a
  pass (also desirable after extra activity by the bot's
  agents).
  - Why: the bot keeps writing session data while the
    command runs, so the invocation's own record plus any
    closing response land after the squash.
  - Safe to repeat: bot session data is append-only, so a
    re-run never conflicts or overwrites. (This could
    change. It is not under the user's control.)
  - No guarantees: events outside the bot's control can leave
    `@` non-empty. The bot's back end may decide to
    squash/consolidate session data, which can take minutes
    and land after the pass. The remedy is the same: just
    run squash-push again. This is why a single pass is never
    guaranteed to leave `@` empty.
- **Nothing to clear after an out-of-band recovery.** Push
  keeps no saved state, so whatever you do to the repos by
  hand is simply the state the next run sees.
- **Late work-repo tweak after the work-repo push succeeded**
  (e.g. updating AGENTS.md or memory) requires `jj
  squash --ignore-immutable` and a re-push. That is a
  remote rewrite and needs explicit approval like any
  push.

## Iterative work

When work for a single commit (the **target**) benefits
from incremental review, loop:

1. `jj new -R .`: fresh empty `@` on top of the target.
2. Make the next round of changes.
3. User reviews the round (see
   [Reviewing changes](#reviewing-changes)).
4. `jj squash -R .` folds into the target and creates a
   new empty `@`.
5. If not done, go to step 2.

Same jj mechanics as a
[sub-cycle ladder](#sub-cycle-ladders), but at
single-commit scope, so the version doesn't change.

## Sub-cycle ladders

When a Work commit subdivides into a sub-cycle (see
[Step naming](#step-naming), and
[versioning.md](versioning.md#suffix-scheme) for how the
manifest's suffix nests), its Work
commits will live as a local jj `@` chain and
**collapse into the sub-cycle's Close-out** before the
parent cycle continues. Ladder commits are scratch, for
review and bisection only.

### Per-Work-commit contract within a ladder

For each Work commit in the ladder:

1. `jj new -R .`: create a fresh empty `@`.
2. Do the commit's work.
3. Run the fast validation (Rust example: `cargo test
   --bins`). **Non-negotiable**, because for code, build and
   clippy alone miss regressions until a later commit runs the
   full suite, raising bisection cost.
4. `jj describe -m "..." -m "..." -R .`: working title
   only. The sub-cycle Close-out collects everything
   into one final commit.

**Nothing here is pushed.** The ladder is local until the
[Close-out squash](#close-out-squash-the-ladder), so no ladder
commit ever carries an `ochid:` trailer: the trailer is stamped
once, by `vc-x1 push`, on the squashed commit. Step 4 is
therefore first-time authoring of a scratch description, not a
rewrite of a published or stamped one, and is the named
exception to
[Re-describing](jj.md#re-describing-coordinate-first-and-keep-the-trailer).

### Navigating the ladder

Common moves:

- `jj log -r '<base>::' -R .`: see the whole ladder
  from its base.
- `jj edit -r <prefix> -R .`: jump `@` to any ladder
  commit by chid prefix, useful for bisection.
- `jj edit @-- -R .`: quick-jump back two commits.
- `jj diff -r <chid> -R .`: review one commit in
  isolation.

Modifications to any ladder commit rewrite it in place, and
descendants auto-rebase.

### Close-out: squash the ladder

When all ladder Work commits are done and tests pass:

```
jj squash --from "<base>..@-" --into @ -u -R .
```

`<base>` is the parent of the first ladder commit, and `-u`
keeps `@`'s description and discards the sources'.
After squash, history is linear (`<base> -> @`), and
intermediate commits are auto-abandoned.

Then `vc-x1 push <bookmark>` as for any other commit. This is
the ladder's first and only publish, and where its `ochid:`
trailer is stamped. The scratch descriptions written at step 4
of the
[per-Work-commit contract](#per-work-commit-contract-within-a-ladder)
never left the machine and never carried one, which is why
describing them freely is safe.

For N = 1 the squash is a no-op (`<base>..@-` is empty
when `@-` is `<base>`). Push the single commit directly.

### Recovery

If a ladder commit goes wrong, back out without losing
prior commits:

- **Discard the current commit.** `jj abandon @ -R .`
  drops it, and you get a fresh empty `@` on the same
  parent.
- **Edit an earlier commit.** `jj edit -r <chid> -R .`,
  make corrections, then `jj edit -r <last-ladder-chid>`
  to return. Descendants auto-rebase.
- **Discard the entire ladder.** `jj op log -R .` shows
  the op history, and `jj op restore <op-id> -R .` reverts
  to that point. Full undo: removes *all* ladder work
  after the chosen op. Use only to start over.

# References

- [`jj.md > Revsets`](jj.md#revsets): revset primitives
  (chid/cid, `@`/`@-`/`@+`, `..`/`::` ranges, prefix matching).
- The per-commit `cargo test --bins` gate exists because a
  regression introduced in an early ladder commit can go
  uncaught until a later commit runs the full suite, raising
  bisection cost.
